q: What is the exact value of cos 105°?
x: cos(60° + 45°) = cos 60° cos 45° − sin 60° sin 45° = √2/4 − √6/4 = (√2 − √6)/4, which is negative as 105° is in the second quadrant. Using + between the products gives (√6 + √2)/4.

q: For every θ, sin(π/2 + θ) equals:
x: sin(π/2 + θ) = sin(π/2) cos θ + cos(π/2) sin θ = cos θ. Check θ = 0: sin(π/2) = 1 = cos 0. The angle π/2 + θ lies in quadrant II for acute θ, where sine is positive, so −cos θ is wrong.

q: For every θ, sin(45° + θ) − cos(45° − θ) equals:
x: sin(45° + θ) = (√2/2)(cos θ + sin θ) and cos(45° − θ) = (√2/2)(cos θ + sin θ), so the difference is 0. The two angles add to 90°, so the sine of one is the cosine of the other.

q: For angles where it is defined, cot(A + B) equals:
o: (cot A cot B + 1)/(cot A + cot B)
(cot A + cot B)/(cot A cot B − 1)
(1 − cot A cot B)/(cot A + cot B)
(cot A cot B − 1)/(cot A + cot B)
x: cot(A + B) = cos(A + B)/sin(A + B) = (cos A cos B − sin A sin B)/(sin A cos B + cos A sin B); dividing top and bottom by sin A sin B gives (cot A cot B − 1)/(cot A + cot B). (cot A cot B + 1)/(cot B − cot A) would be cot(A − B).

q: For every x, sin 3x cos x − cos 3x sin x equals:
x: This is sin(A − B) with A = 3x and B = x, so it equals sin 2x. sin 4x would come from sin(A + B), which has a plus sign.

q: α lies in the second quadrant with sin α = 5/13, and β lies in the fourth quadrant with cos β = 3/5. What is tan(α − β)?
For every θ, cos θ − sin θ equals:
x: √2 cos(θ + π/4) = √2(cos θ · √2/2 − sin θ · √2/2) = cos θ − sin θ. Both √2 cos(θ − π/4) and √2 sin(θ + π/4) expand to cos θ + sin θ.

q: If A + B = 45°, where A and B are acute, what is the value of (1 + tan A)(1 + tan B)?
x: tan(A + B) = 1 gives tan A + tan B = 1 − tan A tan B, so tan A + tan B + tan A tan B = 1. Then (1 + tan A)(1 + tan B) = 1 + (tan A + tan B + tan A tan B) = 2. Check A = 0: 1 × (1 + tan 45°) = 2.

q: What is the value of tan 75° − tan 15°?
x: tan 75° = tan(45° + 30°) = 2 + √3 and tan 15° = tan(45° − 30°) = 2 − √3, so the difference is 2√3. Adding them instead gives 4.

q: Given tan(α + π/4) = 3, what is tan α?
x: tan(α + π/4) = (tan α + 1)/(1 − tan α) = 3, so tan α + 1 = 3 − 3 tan α and tan α = 1/2. Check: (1/2 + 1)/(1 − 1/2) = 3. Using 1 + tan α in the denominator gives 2.

q: For every θ, sin 3θ equals:
x: sin 3θ = sin(2θ + θ) = 2 sin θ cos²θ + (1 − 2 sin²θ) sin θ = 3 sin θ − 4 sin³θ. Check θ = 90°: sin 270° = −1 and 3 − 4 = −1. The form 4 cos³θ − 3 cos θ belongs to cos 3θ.

q: What is the value of 8 sin 15° cos 15° cos 30°?
x: 2 sin 15° cos 15° = sin 30°, so the expression is 4 sin 30° cos 30° = 2 sin 60° = √3. Using sin 2θ = sin θ cos θ (no factor 2) gives √3/2.

q: Given cos θ = 1/8 with 0 < θ < π/2, what is sin(θ/2)?
x: sin²(θ/2) = (1 − cos θ)/2 = (7/8)/2 = 7/16, and θ/2 is acute, so sin(θ/2) = √7/4. 3/4 is cos(θ/2), from (1 + cos θ)/2 = 9/16, and 7/16 forgets the square root.

q: Given tan θ = 1/2, what is tan 3θ?
For angles where it is defined, (1 − cos 2θ)/(1 + cos 2θ) equals:
x: 1 − cos 2θ = 2 sin²θ and 1 + cos 2θ = 2 cos²θ, so the quotient is tan²θ. Swapping the two half-angle forms gives cot²θ.

q: Given sin 2θ = 24/25 with 0 < θ < π/4, what is tan θ?
x: sin 2θ = 2t/(1 + t²) with t = tan θ, so 24t² − 50t + 24 = 0, i.e. 12t² − 25t + 12 = 0, giving t = 3/4 or 4/3. Since θ < π/4, tan θ < 1, so tan θ = 3/4. 4/3 belongs to θ between π/4 and π/2, and 24/7 is tan 2θ.

q: For 0 < θ < π, √[(1 − cos θ)/(1 + cos θ)] equals:
x: 1 − cos θ = 2 sin²(θ/2) and 1 + cos θ = 2 cos²(θ/2), so the root is |tan(θ/2)|, and θ/2 is acute, so it equals tan(θ/2). Check θ = 90°: √(1/1) = 1 = tan 45°.

q: For every θ, sin θ cos θ cos 2θ equals:
x: sin θ cos θ = (1/2) sin 2θ, and (1/2) sin 2θ cos 2θ = (1/4) sin 4θ. Each use of the double-angle formula brings a factor 1/2; using it only once gives (1/2) sin 4θ.

q: With θ = 18°, 2θ = 90° − 3θ, so sin 2θ = cos 3θ. Using this, what is the exact value of sin 18°?
x: 2 sin θ cos θ = 4 cos³θ − 3 cos θ; divide by cos θ: 2 sin θ = 1 − 4 sin²θ, so 4s² + 2s − 1 = 0 and s = (−1 + √5)/4 (positive root). (√5 + 1)/4 is cos 36°, and √(10 − 2√5)/4 is sin 36°.

q: For every x, 2 cos 5x sin x equals:
x: 2 cos A sin B = sin(A + B) − sin(A − B); with A = 5x and B = x this is sin 6x − sin 4x. sin 6x + sin 4x is 2 sin 5x cos x, with the factors the other way round.

q: What is the value of cos 105° + cos 15°?
x: cos C + cos D = 2 cos((C + D)/2) cos((C − D)/2) = 2 cos 60° cos 45° = 2 × 1/2 × √2/2 = √2/2. Using sin 60° in place of cos 60° gives √6/2.

q: What is the value of sin 20° sin 40° sin 80°?
x: sin 40° sin 80° = ½(cos 40° − cos 120°) = ½ cos 40° + ¼. Then sin 20° × that = ¼(sin 60° − sin 20°) + ¼ sin 20° = ¼ sin 60° = √3/8. 1/8 is the value of the cosine product cos 20° cos 40° cos 80°.

q: For every x, sin 4x − sin 2x can be written as:
x: sin C − sin D = 2 cos((C + D)/2) sin((C − D)/2) = 2 cos 3x sin x. 2 sin 3x cos x is the form for sin 4x + sin 2x.

q: What is the value of sin 75° sin 15°?
x: 2 sin A sin B = cos(A − B) − cos(A + B) = cos 60° − cos 90° = 1/2, so sin 75° sin 15° = 1/4. Forgetting to halve gives 1/2.

q: What is the value of cos 15° − sin 15°?
x: sin 15° = cos 75°, so cos 15° − cos 75° = −2 sin 45° sin(−30°) = 2 × √2/2 × 1/2 = √2/2. Check by squaring: 1 − 2 sin 15° cos 15° = 1 − sin 30° = 1/2. √6/2 is cos 15° + sin 15°.

q: A, B and C are the angles of a triangle (A + B + C = π). Which expression equals cos A + cos B + cos C?
x: cos A + cos B = 2 sin(C/2) cos((A − B)/2) and cos C = 1 − 2 sin²(C/2); then cos((A − B)/2) − cos((A + B)/2) = 2 sin(A/2) sin(B/2) gives 1 + 4 sin(A/2) sin(B/2) sin(C/2). Check an equilateral triangle: 3/2 = 1 + 4 × 1/8. 4 cos(A/2) cos(B/2) cos(C/2) is sin A + sin B + sin C.

q: For angles where it is defined, (sin 3x + sin x)/sin 2x equals:
x: sin 3x + sin x = 2 sin 2x cos x, so dividing by sin 2x leaves 2 cos x. Check x = 30°: (1 + 1/2)/(√3/2) = √3 = 2 cos 30°.

q: Given that sin 18° cos 36° = 1/4, what is the value of sin 47° + sin 61° − sin 11° − sin 25°?
x: sin 47° − sin 25° = 2 cos 36° sin 11° and sin 61° − sin 11° = 2 cos 36° sin 25°. Their sum is 2 cos 36°(sin 11° + sin 25°) = 2 cos 36° × 2 sin 18° cos 7° = 4 sin 18° cos 36° cos 7° = cos 7°.
